resources.string: How surfactant works in an alveolus
A simplified cutaway of a normal alveolus. Layers, movements and timing are not to scale. Secretion maintains the film over time; the film spreads and compresses with each breath.

The rounded type II cell stores surfactant, a mixture of lipids and proteins, in layered packets called lamellar bodies. The flat type I cell forms the thin part of the wall through which gases diffuse between air and blood.
A type II cell releases surfactant
A lamellar body fuses with the cell membrane facing the alveolar air. Its contents enter the thin liquid lining, rather than being released directly into the air.
Released surfactant can reach the boundary where alveolar air meets liquid and spread to replenish the existing film. The film lowers surface tension at that boundary.
As the alveolus expands, its air-liquid interface has more area. The existing surfactant film spreads over that larger surface.
As the alveolus gets smaller, the film packs more closely and surface tension falls. Lower tension helps keep the alveolus open at lower lung volumes.
